author: Joseph Conrad
introFa: کتاب «Nostromo» نوشته Joseph Conrad یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Nostromo»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

All that side of the Plaza had been burnt ... a terrible fire, by the light of which I saw the last of the fighting" (476). Were Pushkin not enough to establish a link between "The Bronze Horseman" and the statue in Sulaco's main plaza, we can also turn to Adam Mickiewicz, an activist in the struggle for Polish independence whose work Conrad knew well.3 Mickiewicz had also made friends with the future Decembrists, and published the poem "Oleszkiewicz" prior to the publication of Pushkin's "The Bronze Horseman." Pushkin's poem is, in fact, partly a response to Mickiewicz's. Mickiewicz also treats the St Petersburg flood, which, according to Oleksiy Panych, he saw as "a sign of the future liberation of young Polish Rebels arrested by [the] Tsar and their return to Poland as [a] Promised Land" (1998). Pushkin knew Mickiewicz well, translated some of his poems into Russian, and in 1834 dedicated a poem to him. For his part, Mickiewicz saw the enigmatic gesture of the imperial rider as one of "blessing the Russian people." Just as if, from the top of its artificial cliff (ironically made of Finnish rock), the statue of Peter the Great is showing the way forward to Russia, or, as Pushkin has it, "on your steed you reared up Russia." Pushkin's poem is about the human costs of autocracy, while Mickiewicz sees "The Bronze Horseman" as a symbol of tsarist Russia's intentions towards Poland. In Nostromo, the statue in Sulaco is contrasted with Charles Gould, potentially making Gould a type of emperor or tsar (a Caesar), as his tide "Rey de Sulaco," not always ironically, hints at. For instance, Hernandez addresses Gould: "Caballero ... you are he whom they call the King of Sulaco, the master of the mine? Is it not so?" (357). Gould is linked "with the cause of aristocracy" (47) and his creative activities in the cause of the Gould Concession mirror Peter the Great's talent and audacity: as Pushkin has it in his poem, "Great wonder-worker, you beware!" Much of the initial description of Gould in Part I, Chapter VI is a nod to R. B. Cunninghame Graham and his activities in South America as well as to his legendary horsemanship, which here is contrasted with the un-English style of the campo's riders: 'He ... in a continent posses sing its own style of horsemanship, went on looking thoroughly English even on horseback" (48). Says the narrator: "Charles Gould, to use the 3 For a discussion of Conrad and Mickiewicz, see Szczypien (1998). Cairney 113 suitably lofty phrase, rode like a centaur," or, as Pushkin has it in the poem: "How awesome in the gloom he rides! / There on high, with an arm flung wide, / Behold the image sit, and ride upon his brazen horse astride!" In contrast to the statue of Charles IV, like Gould representing the cause of aristocracy, and riding high and proud on a magnificent horse of stone, the narrator tells us that "the beggars of the town slept on the steps around the pedestal," or as Pushkin has it: "The piteous madman / Fell to prowling about the statue's granite berth." The parallels between the two texts are too many to ignore. Pushkin's poem could be said to describe the clash between nature and humanity, a theme echoed in Gould's wresting the silver from the mountain. Perhaps significant to Gould's character, Pushkin's Peter is not the great conqueror of nature he believed himself to be. "The Bronze Horseman" exudes authority, but Pushkin makes plain his "blasphemous attempt of godlike creation," which echoes in Charles Gould's boundless ambitions to tame nature for political ends. In Pushkin, Peter's "godlike creation" would obscure the very existence of Poland, the "cost of autocracy." In this sense Sulaco is Poland. But then, Gould is unlike Peter, and the allegory is not a simple one. As Pushkin has it: "Proud charger, whither art thou ridden? / Where leadest thou? And where, on whom, wilt plant thy hoof?" Panych points to Peter's "attempt to create an absolutely 'new world'" in defiance of God and history. And the statue of the autocratic tsar is wor shipped ? almost an idol ? and there is Gould ? also in the "New World." Yevgenyi, Pushkin's hero, renounces his noble family and shows an inclination to shuffle off the past, as the people of Sulaco eventually rid themselves of the statue and, by doing so, liberate themselves from their imperialist past. As Pushkin puts it, he "cared not for forbears dead and rotten, / Or antique matters long forgotten." Is this Conrad's mes sage, and a partial explanation for his later refusal of an English (foreign and imperial) knighthood? Charles IV and that other Carlos, Charles Gould are variously linked. As the narrator tells us, "the weather-stained effigy of the mounted king ... seemed to present an inscrutable breast to the political changes which had robbed it of its very name; but neither did the other horseman, well known to the people "keen and alive on his well-shaped, slate-coloured beast with white eye, wear his heart on the sleeve of his This content downloaded from 188.81.93.90 on Sat, 31 May 2014 17:05:46 PM All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

114 Cairney English coat" (49). Where Pushkin and Conrad are concerned, they have the same issues "at heart," if not the same answers. The "Senor Administrador" also has regal trappings, followed by a servant "in a livery of white ... and red." These are the Hapsburg colours, and Conrad's reference to Charles IV, a Bourbon, is to some extent a joke. The policies of Charles III were disastrous for Spain. Charles IV was a cuckold and fool, and in an age of inbred monarchs ruled because Charles II, the last Hapsburg, was physically and mentally disabled. Perhaps this knowledge lies behind the tremendous anticlimax of Part III, Chapter V, where the llaneros from the campo enter the plaza to see the equestrian statue of the King dazzlingly white in the sunshine, towering enormous and motionless above the surges of the crowd, with its eternal gesture of saluting, a murmur of surprise ran through their ranks. 'What is that saint in the big hat?" they asked each other. (385) Conrad's depiction of their politic involvement, one of the ignorant ever exploited by the powerful, forcefully engages the reader, aware that the statue is not a "saint," in a historical reading of the monument. In light of the fictional and constructed Charles IV and the hading of his statue as a "saint," we might suggest that the "saint" recalls "St Petersburg" and connections with "The Bronze Horseman." The colours linked to Gould may also point in this direction. Peter the Great made the first Imperial Russian flag red, blue, and white, basing his choice on the colours of the Duchy of Moscow, gules and argent in Moscow's coat-of-arms, with yet another imperious Russian horseman, a cavalier in white armour rearing on a white horse against a red background. Pushkin, Mickiewicz, and "The Horse of Stone" in Nostromo Christopher Cairney Dogu? University, Istanbul AT THE BEGINNING of Part I, Chapter 6 of Nostromo, the reader is struck by the description of the "equestrian statue of Charles IV at the entrance to the Alameda ... known ... as the Horse of Stone" (48). Keith Carabine has suggested that the statue recalls Manuel Tolsa's famous bronze statue of 1803 of Carlos IV of Spain (1748-1819) in Mexico City (1984: 579).1 Conrad's knowledge of that monument, however, is somewhat less likely than his acquaintance with the famous equestrian statue of Peter the Great in St Petersburg, which "folk of the country" there call "The Bronze Horseman." Conrad, who alludes to that statue in his 1905 essay "Autocracy and War,"2 is likely to have known it through Pushkin's post humously published poem "The Bronze Horseman" (1837) or Adam Mickiewicz's "The Forefather's Eve" (1832) as well as through the popu lar or monthly press, the statue being widely reproduced in photographs. The narrator describes "the weather-stained effigy of the mounted king, with its vague suggestion of a saluting gesture" (49), a gesture thought to be enigmatic and leading to the creation of its own lore and legend. The imposing figure takes on a symbolic temporal solidity amidst the moving masses: a "kingly cavalier reining in his steed on the pedestal above the sleeping [people] ... with his marble arm raised" (48). Later, in Part III, Chapter IV, the narrator describes "the equestrian statue of the 1 The statue is familiarly known as El Caballito (The Little Horse). 2 Cf. "there is no new Russia to take the place of that ill-omened creation which being a fantasy of a madman's brain could in reality be nothing else than a figure out of a nightmare seated upon a monument of fear and oppression" (Notes on Life and Letters 76-77). For a discussion of this allusion, see Bird (1984) and Mroz (1982). This content downloaded from 188.81.93.90 on Sat, 31 May 2014 17:05:46 PM All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

Cairney 111 King dazzlingly ... towering enormous and motionless above the surges of the crowd, with its eternal gesture of saluting" (385). "The Bronze Horseman" in St Petersburg, like Conrad's fictional statue, originally stood in the central square of a pre-revolutionary city, surrounded by the seats of civil and religious power. Catherine the Great commissioned the monument, unveiling E. M. Falconet's masterwork to rapt crowds in August 1782. It clearly symbolized the might of imperial Russia and the continuity of tsardom, and a legend arose that no enemy would take the city whilst it stood in place. As in Nostromo, where "The Horse of Stone" has pride of place in Sulaco's main plaza, the square in which "The Bronze Horseman" stands was a place of military exercise and public merry-making. Given that Pushkin's poem may figure in the background to Nostromo, it seems necessary to consider the statue's specific meaning. While "The Bronze Horseman" was historically seen as protective and leading Russia to the West while resisting Sweden and Finland, Pushkin's interpretation saw Peter the Great in contemporary terms as representing Nicholas I; Russians, in other words, were being trampled under autoc racy's hooves. Pushkin's treatment would probably have had signal appeal to Conrad, and the subject of oppression and revolt has an alle gorical power applicable to partitioned Poland. Additionally, the subject of the personal cost to the revolutionaries of failure and guilt is part of Conrad's family background. Pushkin's poem treats the flooding of the Neva, which engulfed St Petersburg and the base of the statue itself in 1824. However, Pushkin also had friends among the ill-fated Decembrists of 1825 who opposed the tsar. A revolutionary flood, they were beaten back, and it can be said that "The Bronze Horseman" was twice engulfed in a "flood." Pushkin's horseman remains victor over both. Pushkin was fascinated by American democracy and may in the poem cast the contest between the river and the city in 1824 as a battle between the forces of democracy and autoc racy in Russia in 1825. "The Tsarist authorities," who banned the poem during Pushkin's lifetime, found it "anti-autocratic," and Russian censor ship is a large issue here with Conrad remembering the experience of post-partition Poland. In Nostromo, too, Sulaco's main square is eventually a site of revolutionary pilgrimage, the site of the key battle of the revolution, a battle won through blood: "The Plaza. I call it magnificent. 112 Cairney area of Trafalgar Square... The Intendencia, now President's Palace ? Cabildo, where the Lower Chamber of Parliament sits... All that side of the Plaza had been burnt ... a terrible fire, by the light of which I saw the last of the fighting" (476). Were Pushkin not enough to establish a link between "The Bronze Horseman" and the statue in Sulaco's main plaza, we can also turn to Adam Mickiewicz, an activist in the struggle for Polish independence whose work Conrad knew well.3 Mickiewicz had also made friends with the future Decembrists, and published the poem "Oleszkiewicz" prior to the publication of Pushkin's "The Bronze Horseman." Pushkin's poem is, in fact, partly a response to Mickiewicz's. Mickiewicz also treats the St Petersburg flood, which, according to Oleksiy Panych, he saw as "a sign of the future liberation of young Polish Rebels arrested by [the] Tsar and their return to Poland as [a] Promised Land" (1998). Pushkin knew Mickiewicz well, translated some of his poems into Russian, and in 1834 dedicated a poem to him. For his part, Mickiewicz saw the enigmatic gesture of the imperial rider as one of "blessing the Russian people." Just as if, from the top of its artificial cliff (ironically made of Finnish rock), the statue of Peter the Great is showing the way forward to Russia, or, as Pushkin has it, "on your steed you reared up Russia." Pushkin's poem is about the human costs of autocracy, while Mickiewicz sees "The Bronze Horseman" as a symbol of tsarist Russia's intentions towards Poland. In Nostromo, the statue in Sulaco is contrasted with Charles Gould, potentially making Gould a type of emperor or tsar (a Caesar), as his tide "Rey de Sulaco," not always ironically, hints at. For instance, Hernandez addresses Gould: "Caballero ... you are he whom they call the King of Sulaco, the master of the mine? Is it not so?" (357). Gould is linked "with the cause of aristocracy" (47) and his creative activities in the cause of the Gould Concession mirror Peter the Great's talent and audacity: as Pushkin has it in his poem, "Great wonder-worker, you beware!" Much of the initial description of Gould in Part I, Chapter VI is a nod to R. B. Cunninghame Graham and his activities in South America as well as to his legendary horsemanship, which here is contrasted with the un-English style of the campo's riders: 'He ... in a continent posses sing its own style of horsemanship, went on looking thoroughly English even on horseback" (48). Cairney 113 suitably lofty phrase, rode like a centaur," or, as Pushkin has it in the poem: "How awesome in the gloom he rides! / There on high, with an arm flung wide, / Behold the image sit, and ride upon his brazen horse astride!" In contrast to the statue of Charles IV, like Gould representing the cause of aristocracy, and riding high and proud on a magnificent horse of stone, the narrator tells us that "the beggars of the town slept on the steps around the pedestal," or as Pushkin has it: "The piteous madman / Fell to prowling about the statue's granite berth." The parallels between the two texts are too many to ignore. Pushkin's poem could be said to describe the clash between nature and humanity, a theme echoed in Gould's wresting the silver from the mountain. Perhaps significant to Gould's character, Pushkin's Peter is not the great conqueror of nature he believed himself to be. "The Bronze Horseman" exudes authority, but Pushkin makes plain his "blasphemous attempt of godlike creation," which echoes in Charles Gould's boundless ambitions to tame nature for political ends. In Pushkin, Peter's "godlike creation" would obscure the very existence of Poland, the "cost of autocracy." In this sense Sulaco is Poland. But then, Gould is unlike Peter, and the allegory is not a simple one. As Pushkin has it: "Proud charger, whither art thou ridden? / Where leadest thou? And where, on whom, wilt plant thy hoof?" Panych points to Peter's "attempt to create an absolutely 'new world'" in defiance of God and history. And the statue of the autocratic tsar is wor shipped ? almost an idol ? and there is Gould ? also in the "New World." Yevgenyi, Pushkin's hero, renounces his noble family and shows an inclination to shuffle off the past, as the people of Sulaco eventually rid themselves of the statue and, by doing so, liberate themselves from their imperialist past. As Pushkin puts it, he "cared not for forbears dead and rotten, / Or antique matters long forgotten." Is this Conrad's mes sage, and a partial explanation for his later refusal of an English (foreign and imperial) knighthood? Charles IV and that other Carlos, Charles Gould are variously linked. As the narrator tells us, "the weather-stained effigy of the mounted king ... seemed to present an inscrutable breast to the political changes which had robbed it of its very name; but neither did the other horseman, well known to the people "keen and alive on his well-shaped, slate-coloured beast with white eye, wear his heart on the sleeve of his This content downloaded from 188.81.93.90 on Sat, 31 May 2014 17:05:46 PM All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

114 Cairney English coat" (49). Where Pushkin and Conrad are concerned, they have the same issues "at heart," if not the same answers. The "Senor Administrador" also has regal trappings, followed by a servant "in a livery of white ... and red." These are the Hapsburg colours, and Conrad's reference to Charles IV, a Bourbon, is to some extent a joke. The policies of Charles III were disastrous for Spain. Charles IV was a cuckold and fool, and in an age of inbred monarchs ruled because Charles II, the last Hapsburg, was physically and mentally disabled. Perhaps this knowledge lies behind the tremendous anticlimax of Part III, Chapter V, where the llaneros from the campo enter the plaza to see the equestrian statue of the King dazzlingly white in the sunshine, towering enormous and motionless above the surges of the crowd, with its eternal gesture of saluting, a murmur of surprise ran through their ranks. 'What is that saint in the big hat?" they asked each other. (385) Conrad's depiction of their politic involvement, one of the ignorant ever exploited by the powerful, forcefully engages the reader, aware that the statue is not a "saint," in a historical reading of the monument. In light of the fictional and constructed Charles IV and the hading of his statue as a "saint," we might suggest that the "saint" recalls "St Petersburg" and connections with "The Bronze Horseman." The colours linked to Gould may also point in this direction. Peter the Great made the first Imperial Russian flag red, blue, and white, basing his choice on the colours of the Duchy of Moscow, gules and argent in Moscow's coat-of-arms, with yet another imperious Russian horseman, a cavalier in white armour rearing on a white horse against a red background.
